text: You've now seen where cloud security alerts actually come from — Defender for Cloud's plans, GuardDuty, Security Hub's aggregation. This lesson is about what happens once one of those lands in your queue: how to decide what actually matters without either drowning in noise or dismissing something real.

Severity is where you start reading, not where you stop. It's calculated from the alert type alone, with no idea whether the resource it fired on is a disposable sandbox or a production system holding real data. What actually decides urgency is blast radius — what identity, network path, and data that specific resource can reach — combined with asset context. A Medium-severity alert on a production, internet-facing, privileged resource regularly deserves faster action than a High-severity alert on an isolated sandbox.

A handful of patterns account for a huge share of the noise. Your own vulnerability scanner can trigger an SSH brute-force alert. A scheduled backup job running at an odd hour can trigger an impossible-travel alert. A dev or test sandbox with relaxed network rules by design will trip alerts that would be genuinely urgent on production. The fix isn't ignoring these alert types — it's documenting the specific, verified reason for each one and scoping any suppression as narrowly as that explanation allows.

Run the same sequence every time: read the full alert, including its MITRE tactic tag; check whether it's already grouped into an incident or tied to related findings; establish blast radius; rule out a false positive with actual evidence, not a guess; and only then decide. Before closing anything out, correlate the alert's claim against CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log directly, rather than trusting the alerting tool's own summary.

That decision has three real outcomes. Contain immediately when you've confirmed malicious activity with a meaningful blast radius. Monitor when confidence or blast radius is low. Escalate anything the first five steps didn't let you resolve confidently — escalating isn't a failure of triage, it's what the sequence is there to catch.

That closes out cloud-native tooling and the habit of actually triaging what it produces. Next, this course moves from detecting and responding to protecting the data itself — encryption at rest and in transit, and exactly who holds the key on each cloud.
